title: Big-Button TV Remotes for Parents and Grandparents: Simple Picks and What They Can't Do
subtitle: A plain-English guide to large, backlit universal remotes that make watching TV less of a puzzle, plus the limits worth knowing before you give one as a gift.
excerpt: If the TV remote has too many tiny buttons, a big-button universal remote can help. Here is how they work, what to check before you buy, and three options priced from $15.99 up to $55.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Today's TV remotes can feel like they were built for someone with sharp eyes and nimble fingers. The buttons are small, the labels are faint, and in a dim living room it is easy to press the wrong one and end up on a screen nobody recognizes.

A big-button universal remote is a small, practical fix. It puts the buttons people actually use, like power, volume and channel, front and center, often with a light so they show up in the dark. For a parent or grandparent who just wants to turn on the news, it can be a thoughtful gift.

A universal remote is one remote that can be set up to control more than one device, such as a TV and a cable box. The models below use infrared, an invisible light signal, so you need to point the remote at the device with nothing in the way. An infrared remote can only control devices that accept infrared commands.
The tricky part is usually setup, which means teaching the remote which TV it is talking to. Darragh Murphy of Tom's Guide (September 30, 2026) wrote that:
"programming a universal remote is often the hardest part of any of these systems" — Darragh Murphy, Tom's Guide, September 30, 2026

That is why the remotes below lean on simple setup. The Philips MotionGlow model uses what Philips calls OneTouch setup: you put in the batteries and press the button for your TV's brand, instead of entering long codes. Both Philips models are preprogrammed for Samsung, LG, Sony, Vizio and Roku TVs. The product pages do not say how other TV brands are set up. A different approach is a pared-down remote with only a handful of buttons, which can suit someone who gets confused by extra choices.

items: Your TV brand. Check that the brand is on the remote's preprogrammed list. If it is not, confirm with the seller before buying.
How many devices it controls. A TV plus a cable box is one thing. A TV, soundbar, cable box and streaming player all in use may need more than a two-device remote.
A light for dark rooms. Backlit buttons glow so they are easier to see in the evening. The MotionGlow model turns its light on when you pick it up.
Big, clearly colored keys. Large volume and channel buttons in distinct colors are easier to find by sight and by feel.
Batteries. The Philips pages list two AA batteries. The MindCare listing says three AAA batteries, not included. Have a set on hand either way.
Model number. Similar-sounding remotes can differ in features and price, so buy by model number, not by name alone.

Support and returns. Phone help is useful if setup gets stuck; Jasco lists a line for its Philips remotes (details below). Check the store's return policy in case the remote does not work with the TV.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well

If you are giving one as a gift, consider setting it up yourself during a visit. For the MotionGlow model, that means putting in two AA batteries and pressing the button for the TV's brand. Then test the basics together: power, volume, channels and mute.
One suggestion: keep the old remote somewhere handy, such as a drawer with a small sticky label, until you are sure the new one does everything your parent needs.

None of these product pages list buttons for streaming apps like Netflix. Tom's Guide notes that streaming support depends on both the remote and the streaming player, so check the maker's compatibility list if a streaming box is part of the setup. The MotionGlow's AUX button is preset for Roku boxes, and it can be reprogrammed for a soundbar, cable box or other device. A remote also cannot fix trouble hearing or seeing the TV; if that is the real issue, a doctor or audiologist is the right place to start.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A simpler remote will not change everything about how a TV works, but it can take a daily frustration off the table. Pick one that matches the TV brand, set it up together, and enjoy the next show without the hunt for the right button.

products.name: Philips OneTouch Big Button MotionGlow Universal Remote (SRP3415B/37)
products.blurb: A different model, with a different price, from the 2-device Philips remote below. It suits someone watching in a dim room: the backlight turns on when the remote is picked up, and the extra-large buttons include colorblind-friendly volume and channel keys. It is preprogrammed for Samsung, LG, Sony, Vizio and Roku TVs, and the page lists free U.S.-based tech support.

products.name: Philips OneTouch Universal Remote, 2-Device, Big Buttons, Backlit (SRP3945B/37)
products.blurb: A budget pick for a TV plus one other device, with a fully backlit keypad and large blue volume and orange channel buttons. It adds play/pause, fast forward and rewind for smart TVs and streaming players. Phone support is listed Monday to Friday, 7am to 6pm Central, at (800) 654-8483.

products.name: MindCare Senior TV Remote (MC-0036)
products.blurb: Suits someone who does best with very few choices: it has five favorite-channel buttons, large volume and channel rockers, and can be set to show only the most-used buttons. It works with TV, cable or satellite boxes that use a standard infrared remote and takes three AAA batteries, which the listing says are not included. Availability unverified; one other retailer's listing reads Discontinued, so confirm before ordering.
